summary: Suggests a change in how FTP client programs behave, so FTP works better through firewalls. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: FTP normally lets the server open a data connection back to the client. This memo recommends using PASV so the client opens that connection, which can work better with packet-filter firewalls.

questions: why does ftp not work through firewalls
what is the ftp pasv command
subtitle: A recommendation to use FTP PASV so clients open data connections through firewalls.

tldr.problem: FTP's server-initiated data connections can look like incoming calls to random client ports, which packet-filter firewalls may block.
tldr.mechanism: With PASV, the server opens a passive port and tells the client where to connect; the client then opens the data connection.
tldr.outcome: The memo recommends that FTP clients use PASV instead of PORT. It also outlines an optional APSV command that it says had not been implemented.

today: RFC 1579 is Informational and describes a suggested change to FTP client behavior. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FTP Data Connections Trouble Firewalls
sections.content:
FTP uses a second TCP connection to transfer files. By default, the server opens this connection to the client. Packet-filter firewalls generally cannot permit incoming calls to arbitrary port numbers.

The memo says most clients instead open a new connection for each transfer, choose a new port to avoid TCP's TIMEWAIT state and announce it with the PORT command. This still causes an incoming request to an unknown port. Blocking only ports below 1024 is risky because the memo notes that dangerous services such as X Windows use higher-numbered ports.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP file data uses a separate connection. A connection opened by the server can arrive at a random client port that a firewall blocks.

sections.title: How PASV Changes the Connection
sections.content:
With the PASV command, the FTP server listens on a port and tells the client its number. The client then opens the TCP connection to that server port. The memo says outgoing calls present fewer problems for firewalls.

Some servers do not honor PASV and return a 500 Command not understood reply. A client can fall back to current behavior, although the memo notes that the transfer may still not work through a firewall.
sections.plainLanguage: PASV tells the server to wait on a port and report that port to the client. The client then starts the data connection to the server.

sections.title: Client Recommendation and APSV Proposal
sections.content:
The memo recommends that vendors change FTP clients, including FTP proxy agents such as Gopher daemons, to use PASV instead of PORT. It recommends PASV even for transfers that do not cross a firewall. It also points to RFC 1123 for guidance on the PASV response format.

As a possible protocol enhancement, the client could send APSV, meaning all passive, at startup. A server supporting it would use passive opens by default and return a proposed 151 reply containing the port for a transfer. The memo says APSV had not been implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: The author recommends PASV for FTP clients. APSV is a separate proposed command for choosing passive connections by default, and the memo reports no implementation.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The memo notes concerns about packet-filter configuration and about allowing arbitrary outgoing calls. It says PASV can improve gateway security because client-side gateways no longer need to create ports that outsiders might contact before the real FTP client.

The server must accept calls to random data ports. The author argues this is manageable because there are fewer FTP servers than clients, allowing filters to permit access to selected servers and those servers to use high-numbered ports for data.
sections.plainLanguage: PASV changes which side accepts a connection. The memo says server-side ports can be managed because there are fewer FTP servers than clients.
